title: The AI compute bottleneck is no longer GPU—Huang says it's memory
dek: Huang said three years ago he already explained the future memory demand curve to Micron and SK Hynix; this supply tightness is not the historical cyclical memory price fluctuation but structural change in AI compute architecture.
why: The substance of this episode is concentrated in the last twelve minutes: structural analysis of the memory bottleneck, clarification on why H200 wasn't discussed in China—both hard information; the customer cases at the start can be skipped.
who: Founders and investors tracking enterprise AI infrastructure investment, compute supply chain trajectory, or wanting to understand NVIDIA's nuance in its China positioning.
skip: The opening chat about customer numbers can be fast-forwarded; it doesn't affect understanding the hard information that follows.

points.h: AI factory customers are moving from pilot to production
points.body: Dell added 1,000 AI factory customers this year, bringing the total to 5,000. Michael Dell stressed the key change is not quantity but stage—customers are transitioning from testing and evaluation to true production deployment, with 1,000-GPU-scale operations like Eli Lilly and Samsung. These are real-world implementations in the physical world, not screen-based demonstrations.

points.h: Intelligence must run where data is generated
points.body: Jensen explained why enterprise AI should run locally rather than in the cloud: intelligence must be produced where context happens, because enterprise data, proprietary knowledge, and security requirements are on-premises. He distinguished ChatGPT from agentic AI—ChatGPT is great but only generates content; agentic AI actually does work, which is the value enterprises will pay for.

points.h: CPU became the harness for agentic AI
points.body: NVIDIA introduced Vera CPU. Jensen defined it as the harness for agentic AI—equipping the large language model brain with memory, networking, and tool-calling ability to become a truly functional digital robot. NVIDIA builds the brain (Grace Blackwell, Vera Rubin) and long-term memory architecture; Dell integrates these technical components into enterprise-ready solutions, with the product called Dell AI Data Platform.

points.h: The bottleneck has shifted from GPU to memory
points.body: Asked what the biggest supply bottleneck is now, Jensen's first answer was memory, followed by advanced-node semiconductors. He said this is not traditional cyclical memory pricing—three years ago he already explained the future demand curve to Micron's Sanjay Mitra and SK Hynix, who adjusted their capacity plans accordingly. So this supply-chain tightness looks more like a structural uplift driven by AI demand.

points.h: Digital agents lead to physical agents
points.body: Jensen compared agents to digital employees: today there are a billion people working worldwide; in the future, hundreds of billions of AI agents will run 24/7, each needing a computer and storage space like an employee. He believes this AI infrastructure buildout will take at least a decade-plus because after digital agents comes much larger-scale physical AI—robots entering real industry. Supply chains have roughly doubled or quadrupled year-over-year for years and still can't meet demand.

points.h: He didn't personally discuss H200 in China
points.body: Asked whether H200 can be sold to Chinese customers, Jensen stated clearly that on this China trip he didn't directly discuss H200 with Chinese officials. He attended representing the U.S. in support of President Trump; the specific decision depends on what the President and Chinese leaders work out. He personally judges China's AI demand is similarly vast and will likely be more open long-term, but that's just his personal sense, not a promise in hand. Michael Dell added that Dell has business in China and observes all export controls, hoping for more economic cooperation between the two countries.

points.h: Taiwan remains the global tech manufacturing and R&D center
points.body: When the host pressed on China's hard-line position on Taiwan, Jensen didn't comment on politics and stressed he wasn't part of presidential-level dialogue. What he addressed was supply chain: Taiwan remains the center for global tech manufacturing and R&D; TSMC's capacity is still critical. Meanwhile, the U.S. is reindustrializing, building more chip fabs, packaging plants, and computer factories to increase supply-chain diversity and resilience—not to replace Taiwan's role.

points.h: NVIDIA and Dell hint they'll collaborate on GPU-powered PCs
points.body: The host directly asked if NVIDIA and Dell would launch personal computers with built-in powerful GPUs; both said they can't disclose plans yet but will announce soon. Jensen took the opportunity to lay out his view of the PC's end state: computing went from mainframes to personal computers; now it's moving from cloud AI to personal AI. AI needs to run where data and scenarios happen—laptops, factories, hospital operating rooms, and autonomous vehicles all need local agents, not just cloud dependency.
